messages.content: Can you give me 95% confidence interval for a sample mean with standard deviation of 10, sample size of 50 and sample mean of 25? And can you do the same but for a sample size of 150 instead?

function.name: confidence_interval_calculate
function.description: Calculate the confidence interval for a mean. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

sample_std_dev.description: The standard deviation of the sample.

confidence_level.description: The level of confidence. Default is 0.9. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Sure!  
Below I’ll walk through how to get the **95 % confidence intervals** for the sample means when  

| Scenario | Sample Size \(n\) | Standard Deviation \(\sigma_s\) | Mean \(\bar{x}\) |
|----------|-------------------|---------------------------------|------------------|
| A        | 50                | 10                              | 25               |
| B        | 150               | 10                              | 25               |

---

### Which formula should we use?

Because only a *sample* standard deviation (\(s = 10\)) was supplied – not a true population σ – it’s safest to treat this as an estimation problem and use the **Student‑t distribution** rather than the normal (z) distribution.  
The general form for a one–tailed 95 % CI around a sample mean is

\[
\boxed{\;\bar x \pm t_{\frac{α}{2},\,ν}\,\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\;}
\]

where  

* \(t_{\frac{α}{2},\,ν}\) is the critical t‑value at significance α/2 with ν degrees of freedom (here \(ν = n - 1\)).  
* \(α = 0.05\) for a 95 % CI → \(α/2 = 0.025\).  

If you prefer the simpler normal approximation, just replace the t‑critical with the z‑critical \(z_{0.025}=1.959964\). Both approaches will yield very similar results because our samples are reasonably sized.

---

## 1️⃣  Confidence Interval for \(n = 50\)

| Step | Calculation | Result |
|------|-------------|--------|
| Degrees of Freedom | \(ν = n-1 = 49\) | — |
| Critical t‑value | \(t_{0.025,49} ≃ 2.010\) | — |
| Standard Error | \(SE = \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{50}} ≃ 1.41421\) | — |
| Margin of Error | \(ME = t × SE = 2.010 × 1.41421 ≃ 2.8445\) | — |
| Lower Bound | \(\bar{x}-ME = 25 - 2.8445 ≃ 22.156\) | — |
| Upper Bound | \(\bar{x}+ME = 25 + 2.8445 ≃ 27.844\) | — |

> **Result:**  
> \[
> \textbf{95 % CI}_{n=50}: \quad (22.16,\; 27.84)
> \]
> 
> *(Rounded to two decimal places.)*

*(Using the normal z‑critical would give a slightly tighter interval: (22.23, 27.77), differing by less than 0.02 on each side.)*

---

## 2️⃣  Confidence Interval for \(n = 150\)

| Step | Calculation | Result |
|------|-------------|--------|
| Degrees of Freedom | \(ν = n-1 = 149\) | — |
| Critical t‑value | \(t_{0.025,149} ≃ 1.978\) | — |
| Standard Error | \(SE = \dfrac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \dfrac{10}{\sqrt{150}} ≃ 0.816496\) | — |
| Margin of Error | \(ME = t × SE = 1.978 × 0.816496 ≃ 1.6148\) | — |
| Lower Bound | \(\bar{x}-ME = 25 - 1.6148 ≃ 23.385\) | — |
| Upper Bound | \(\bar{x}+ME = 25 + 1.6148 ≃ 26.615\) | — |

> **Result:**  
> \[
> \textbf{95 % CI}_{n=150}: \quad (23.39,\; 26.62)
> \] 

*(Again, if you used the normal z‑critical you'd obtain (23.40, 26.60)—virtually identical.)*

---

### Quick Summary Table

| Sample Size | 95 % CI (t‑based) | 95 % CI (normal z‑based) |
|------------|--------------------|---------------------------|
| 50         | (22.16, 27.84)     | (22.23, 27.77)            |
| 150        | (23.39, 26.62)     | (23.40, 26.60)            |

Both sets of intervals convey essentially the same information—your sample mean of 25 lies within roughly ±2.85 units when \(n=50\) and within about ±1.61 units when \(n=150\), reflecting increased precision with larger data.

Let me know if you’d like the calculations shown step‑by‑step in code, or anything else clarified!
